messages.subject: Combing density estimates and SE, lcl, ucl
messages.subject_clean: Combing density estimates and SE, lcl, ucl
messages.body_plain:
Hello secr users,

We are running series of simulations to
assess the effect of modelling (and failing to model) sex and spatial variation
in SECR parameter estimates on density estimates. We have 2 trap arrays
within 3 unique study areas (each array samples distinct populations), where
parameters (D, g0, sigma) vary for each area and sex. We are using a
multi-session capthist object (with a total of 12 sessions- 2 traplines x male
and female x 3 areas) fit using full likelihood (as we are interested in
modeling density covariates in the future we are not using conditional
likelihood). sessioncov is used to model the effects of both
sex and area. We are aware that sex can also be modelled using either
individual covariates or groups. Everything is run on secr v
4.3.1.

The challenge we are having is estimating
total density (for both sexes by area) and it’s SE, ucl and lcl using predict,
which, by default, presents 12 session-specific estimates. We would prefer
to present estimates of total density (both sexes) within study areas, but have
not been able to using the newdata argument. Similarly, we
were unable to achieve this using derived and the groups argument
(which seems to be consistent with the documentation – if using fully
likelihood models using g (groups) will not be handled
correctly?).

Any suggestions are much appreciated.

Thank you in advance,

Brynn

messages.subject: Re: Combing density estimates and SE, lcl, ucl
messages.subject_clean: Combing density estimates and SE, lcl, ucl
messages.body_plain:
Hello Brynn
I think you can tackle this by controlling how factor covariates are coded with the details option 'contrasts'. There are some relevant notes in Section 7.8 of https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/openCR-vignette.pdf. The idea is to code the covariate so that one beta parameter corresponds to the mean (but note caveat in Section 7.8). The same option is available in 'secr'. Example below (replace 'session' with 'sex' in your case).
Murray

library(secr)
msk <- make.mask(traps(ovenCHp[[1]]), buffer = 250, nx = 25)
setNumThreads(7)
fit <-secr.fit(ovenCHp,model = D~session, details =
        list(contrasts = list(session = contr.sum)))
# extract
meanD <- exp(coef(fit)['D',c('beta','lcl','ucl')])
est <- do.call(rbind, lapply(predict(fit),'[',1,))
# plot
par(mar=c(4,5,2,2))
plot(2005:2009, est$estimate, ylim=c(0,3), pch=16, xlab='',
    ylab= expression(paste('Density', ~~ha^-1)))
segments(2005:2009, est$lcl, 2005:2009, est$ucl)
abline(h=meanD, lty=c(1,2,2), col='red')

R version 4.0.2/secr 4.3.1.

Any suggestions are much appreciated.

Thanks

Roland

messages.subject: Estimation of male roe deer density - model mK 'site transient response'
messages.subject_clean: Estimation of male roe deer density - model mK 'site transient response'
messages.body_plain:
Dear secr community,

We are doing a study to estimate the density of male roe deer in 1km2 of forest using 20 photo traps.  The data were analysed using secr and different predefined models on the baseline encounter probability (g0) were tested while keeping the movement parameter σ constant and constant values of the animal density D. Models were compared using the Akaike information criterion (AIC).

Model selection reveals substantial evidence for the ‘site transient response’ model MK.

I can't really understand what this MK model means...?

Does it mean that the efficiency of the site depends on a previous capture?

Maybe someone could help me to understand a little bit better what this mK model is and what it represents at the biological (applied) level?

Thanks,

Best regards,

Inès

messages.subject_clean: Estimation of male roe deer density - model mK 'site transient response'
messages.body_plain:
The vignette secr-overview.pdf defines the predictors 'k' and 'K' as follows
k -  site effectiveness changes once any animal caught
K - site effectiveness depends on preceding occasion

I don't know of any real life application. Perhaps odour may linger in a trap affecting the later probability of catching any animal (though you might think self-odour and other-odour would have different effects). I can't imagine an application to automatic cameras, and if that model is the best by AIC I would suspect it is just a surrogate for some other heterogeneity.
Murray

messages.subject: How to change color palette in plot.capthist?
messages.subject_clean: How to change color palette in plot.capthist?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm sorry to bother everyone with such a simple question, but I have tried everything I could think of and I didn't manage to change the color palette in plot.capthist when plotting the type = "n.per.detector". I would like to change the colors, but also adjust it to the maximum number of animals per detector in the data set (not the maximum number of individuals as it is coded at the moment).

Below is some example code to show what I mean:

####################################
####################################
#load library
library("secr")

# Code adapted from example in package's R documentation

testregion <- data.frame(x = c(0,200,200,0),
                         y = c(0,0,200,200))
popn <- sim.popn (D = 10, core = testregion, buffer = 0,
                  model2D = "hills", details = list(hills = c(-1,0.5)))
t1 <- make.grid(nx = 1, ny = 1)
t1.10 <- make.systematic (cluster = t1, spacing = 10,
                           region = testregion)
capt <- sim.capthist(t1.100, popn = popn, noccasions = 40)

## now plot captures ...
temp <- plot(capt, title = "Individuals per detector",
             type = "n.per.detector", hidetraps = TRUE,gridspace = 10,border = 1,
             gridlines = TRUE, cappar = list(cex = 1))

#How can I change the color palette in the above plot() function?
#Also: in plot function the color palette seems to depend on the maximum number possible per detector
#not the maximum number present in the data set.

## add legend - I think a gradient legend works best for this type of graph
library(plotrix)
color.legend(-20,200,-10,100,legend=temp$legend,rect.col=rev(temp$colour),gradient="y",cex=0.8)

####################################
####################################

It would be really great if someone could tell me how to do that! And again sorry for such a superficial, not statistics-related, question!

Cheers,
Lukas

messages.subject: Re: empirical.varD
messages.body_plain:
Hi Manvi,

Probably much to late to be useful, sorry I missed this post.
Answer to question 1 is "yes", if any information is shared when estimating parameters
2. I believe this is possible, but may require you to refit models and set contrasts.
3. If meaningful spatial covariates are available, results are likely to be more useful, and more precise. We struggle to identify useful covariates except at large spatial scales, due to lack of spatial resolution in anthropogenic mortality data, and bears' feeding behaviour (seasonal "migration" to abundant food, making it hard to quantify habitat quality within home ranges.)

Eric

We are running a series of models with a number of spatial covariates on D and various combinations of bk and h2 on sigma and g0.  The AICs for the models for bk or h2 on sigma or g0 are a lot higher than for the g0~1 or sigma~1 models, yet the beta parameters indicate support for h2 and bk (95% CIs exclude zero).  I am not sure whether to go with AIC or the 95% CIs for model selection.  Any ideas?  Thanks!
Joe

messages.subject: Re: AIC results confusing
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe
I've pondered this but I don't have a good answer. From your description it's more than just a problem with mixture models and their known multimodality?  If you usually rely on AIC and the information theoretic approach then you'll want to stick with it, but I sense that you distrust the maximized likelihoods and hence AIC.

Thinking some more: it could be that the ~1 models are being fit using the 'fastproximity' algorithm of secr 4.x  that messes with the data (collapses occasions) and gives the same estimates but different likelihood. You can suppress that with details = list(fastproximity = FALSE) - worth doing this with the g0~1, sigma~1 models to see if it makes a difference.

Otherwise: It might be worth checking the beta parameter SEs by evaluating again with the alternate algorithm (i.e. run secr.fit(... method = 'none', start = oldmodelfit)). In principle you could check SE with a parametric bootstrap, but the canned simulation methods do not work for all models.

Murray
